title: Continuous annealing of medium-Mn steels: diffusion-limited austenite reversion under carbide-induced chemical heterogeneity
abstract: The effect of pre-tempering on austenite reversion during intercritical annealing of a 1.6 Al medium-Mn steel was investigated, with particular emphasis on the role of carbide-induced chemical heterogeneity. Contrary to the commonly assumed chemically homogeneous initial condition, pre-tempering produces Mn- and C-enriched carbides, leading to pronounced local compositional gradients prior to annealing. The results indicate that this heterogeneity alters the balance between austenite nucleation and growth. While nucleation is promoted at carbide–matrix interfaces, austenite growth becomes locally constrained due to Mn depletion in the surrounding matrix and limited substitutional diffusion. As a result, the transformation appears to proceed in a spatially non-uniform manner, leading to the formation of fragmented and partially transformed regions rather than a continuous austenite network. Despite a comparable retained austenite fraction (∼25–30%), the pre-tempered condition exhibits significantly reduced grain size and loss of morphological continuity, accompanied by increased austenite stability and altered strain hardening behavior. These findings provide evidence for a diffusion-limited, spatially heterogeneous transformation pathway, in which carbide-induced chemical gradients and restricted solute transport lead to locally arrested austenite growth. The results provide new insights into the coupling between chemical heterogeneity, transformation kinetics, and microstructural continuity, and highlight the importance of initial microstructural and chemical state in controlling phase transformation pathways in medium-Mn steels.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Medium-Mn steels are currently among the most promising alloys of the new generation of Advanced High-Strength Steels (AHSS) [ 1–3 ]. Depending on the targeted mechanical properties, they can be processed by quenching and partitioning [ 4 ], austempering [ 5 ], or intercritical annealing [ 6 ]. The latter heat treatment enables the formation of the highest fraction of stable retained austenite (RA), resulting in superior ductility while maintaining high strength [ 7 ]. With increasing Mn concentration, the achievable fraction of stable RA increases, leading to further improvement in the mechanical properties [ 6 , 8 , 9 ]. However, higher Mn contents are also associated with several undesirable effects, including increased alloy cost and technological challenges related to microsegregation [ 10 , 11 ], hydrogen embrittlement [ 12 ], reduced hole expansion ratio [ 13 , 14 ], and increased hot-working resistance [ 15 ].

So far, aside from alloy composition design, the intercritical annealing process has primarily been described in terms of soaking temperature and time [ 16–19 ], as these parameters provide clear and straightforward control over process outcomes. Increasing both the soaking temperature and time leads to a higher fraction of austenite, but simultaneously reduces its stability. A proper control of the time–temperature combination allows achieving up to ∼40% RA with sufficient stability to ensure a gradual strain-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) during deformation.

The literature is still dominated by studies based on so-called batch annealing conditions, typically involving soaking times ranging from several to several tens of hours [ 7 , 20 , 21 ]. Such long soaking times are applied to obtain a high fraction of austenite sufficiently enriched in C and Mn under near-equilibrium conditions [ 7 , 22 ]. Although this approach provides valuable insight into phase transformation mechanisms and equilibrium partitioning phenomena, they do not reflect modern industrial processing conditions for steel sheet production.

On the other hand, increasing attention has recently been devoted to flash annealing approaches applied to medium-Mn steels [ 23 ]. These methods utilize extremely high heating rates, often reaching several hundred °C s −1  through induction heating, combined with soaking times of only a few seconds and subsequent rapid cooling. Under such conditions, a high fraction of stable RA is achieved primarily through rapid C partitioning and significant grain refinement, whereas Mn redistribution remains limited due to insufficient diffusion time [ 24 , 25 ]. Although scientifically attractive, such processing routes are difficult to integrate with currently employed continuous annealing technologies used in industrial sheet production.

At present, continuous annealing represents the most widely used heat treatment route in industrial sheet steel production, making the adaptation of newly developed medium-Mn steels to such processing conditions essential for their practical implementation. Continuous annealing typically involves moderate heating rates ranging from several to several tens of °C s −1  and soaking times usually not exceeding ∼100 s. However, despite its clear industrial relevance, continuous intercritical annealing of medium-Mn steels has so far received significantly less attention than conventional batch annealing approaches, largely due to the long-standing assumption that annealing times below approximately 2 min are insufficient to enable substantial Mn redistribution and stabilization of RA [ 26 , 27 ]. Consequently, the number of studies performed under such conditions remains limited [ 28–30 ]. Nevertheless, the available results indicate that comparable mechanical properties and RA fractions can be achieved even at substantially reduced processing times [ 30–32 ].

Previous studies [ 8 , 33 , 34 ] have also frequently focused on the effect of the initial deformation state on the process. The standard processing route for steel sheets involves hot rolling followed by cold rolling. Intercritical annealing of cold-rolled steels involves recrystallization of deformed martensite as well as austenite reverse transformation (ART) at martensite grain boundaries [ 35 ]. As a result, a dual-phase microstructure with a globular morphology is formed, primarily due to recrystallization. This microstructure has several drawbacks, the most important being the presence of a pronounced yield point, resulting from the significant strength mismatch between ferrite and RA. Therefore, recent studies increasingly introduce an additional austenitization step after hot rolling to obtain a non-deformed, plate-like martensitic microstructure prior to intercritical annealing (similar to that in hot-rolled material). Eliminating recrystallization during subsequent intercritical annealing enables the formation of an elongated ferrite and RA morphology inherited from martensite, which contributes to the suppression of a distinct yield point during tensile deformation [ 36 ].

Despite extensive studies on intercritical annealing of medium-Mn steels, the transformation is commonly interpreted assuming a chemically homogeneous initial state and continuous austenite growth governed by bulk diffusion and local equilibrium conditions [ 8 ]. The present work challenges this assumption by considering the effect of pre-tempering-induced chemical heterogeneity associated with the formation of Mn-enriched carbides under industrially relevant continuous annealing conditions. Particular attention is devoted to the role of local compositional gradients in modifying the austenite reversion pathway, especially under conditions of limited transformation time and non-equilibrium partitioning. Furthermore, the possible contribution of Al redistribution is also considered due to its strong ferrite-stabilizing effect. In this context, the present study investigates the relationship between carbide-induced chemical heterogeneity, RA morphology, and transformation behavior using combined EBSD, TEM/HR-TEM, dilatometry, and mechanical testing.

sections.heading: Material
paragraphs:
The chemical composition of the Al-alloyed medium-Mn steel investigated in this study is presented in  Table 1 
                         . The Mn content was set at 5 wt% to achieve a balance between mechanical performance, cost, and industrial manufacturability, as discussed in detail elsewhere [ 31 ]. The carbon content was intentionally kept low to reduce its detrimental impact on weldability [ 37 ]. Silicon and aluminum were introduced to suppress carbide formation; however, silicon was largely substituted by aluminum to enhance hot-dip galvanizing performance [ 38 ], and reduce slightly density [ 39 ]. Mo was used to increase strength due to solid solution strengthening, grain refinement, and precipitation strengthening. The alloy was melted in a Balzers vacuum furnace to achieve high metallurgical cleanliness. A 25 kg ingot was subsequently forged and hot-rolled to a final thickness of 4.5 mm, with a finishing temperature of 750 °C [ 40 ].

sections.heading: Heat treatment
paragraphs:
To investigate the influence of the prior microstructural state on the microstructure and mechanical properties of intercritically annealed medium-Mn steels, two thermal cycles were designed ( Fig. 1 
                         ). The first involved austenitization in the austenitic region followed by rapid cooling to obtain a fully martensitic microstructure (“Q” sample). This quenching step was followed by intercritical annealing at 710 °C for 40 s to produce a ferrite–austenite duplex microstructure (“Q 710” sample).

In the second thermal cycle, an additional tempering step was introduced after quenching, involving holding at 600 °C for 3 h to obtain a strongly tempered microstructure (“T” sample). The tempered material was subsequently subjected to intercritical annealing (“T710” sample). The intercritical annealing parameters were selected based on prior optimization reported in Ref. [ 31 ]. The heating rate of 3 °C/s was selected, as it is both achievable under industrial conditions [ 41 ] (heating zone) and allows for a diffusive ART process. The 40 s soaking time provides a favorable combination of high RA fraction and enhanced mechanical properties [ 31 ], while remaining compatible with industrial continuous annealing line conditions. Cooling at 10 °C/s does not trigger any phase transformation.

sections.heading: Dilatometry
paragraphs: Physical simulations and heat treatment experiments were performed using a BÄHR DIL805A/D high-resolution dilatometer. Cylindrical samples (4 mm in diameter and 10 mm in length) were machined parallel to the rolling direction. Heating was carried out by induction, while dimensional changes were monitored using an LVDT system equipped with fused silica pushrods. Temperature was controlled by an S-type thermocouple spot-welded at the center of the specimen. Heating and soaking were conducted under vacuum to avoid oxidation, whereas cooling was performed using helium gas. The analysis of dilatometric data followed ASTM  A1033-04  [ 42 ], with transformation start points identified as deviations from linearity in the dilatation curves [ 43 ]. The sub-size tensile specimens were also heat-treated in the dilatometer according to methodology proposed in Ref. [ 32 ] to ensure precise thermal control.

Heat treatment conditions were identical to those used in dilatometric experiments. Tensile tests were conducted on a ZWICK Z020 testing machine at a strain rate of 10 −3  s −1 , with strain measured using an extensometer. Microhardness measurements were carried out using an FB-700 tester under a 1 kgf load. Ten indentations were performed per sample; the extreme values were excluded, and the average was calculated from the remaining results.

sections.heading: Microstructure characterization
paragraphs: Specimens from dilatometric tests were prepared using standard metallographic procedures, including grinding up to 1200 grit, polishing with 3 μm and 1 μm abrasives, and final OPU polishing. For SEM observations, samples were etched with 3% nital. Microstructural characterization was performed using a Zeiss SUPRA 35 SEM in secondary electron mode at 20 kV and a working distance of 10 mm. Detailed crystallographic analysis was conducted using EBSD on an FEI Quanta FEG 450 microscope. Measurements were performed at 20 kV with a 70° tilt and probe current of ∼2.5 nA. Data processing was carried out using OIM TSL software (v. 7.3.1). A two-step cleaning procedure was applied, including grain confidence index standardization and neighbor orientation correlation [ 46 ]. Points with CI ≤ 0.1 were excluded, and the final dataset showed less than 4% modification after cleaning. Image quality (IQ) and phase maps were used to identify microstructural constituents. Final verification was performed using TEM. TEM-EDS analysis was employed to assess chemical elements distribution in the microstructure. Observations were carried out on a TITAN 80-300 microscope operating at 300 kV, equipped with advanced imaging and spectroscopy systems. Transmission Kikuchi Diffraction (TKD) was performed using an EDAX Velocity Pro camera in a high-resolution SEM, allowing for the characterization of electron-transparent specimens. By capturing diffraction patterns from transmitted rather than backscattered electrons, this technique overcomes the spatial resolution limits of conventional EBSD and enables precise orientation mapping at the nanoscale with a resolution better than 10 nm. The volume fraction of RA was determined by XRD using Co-Kα radiation on a Bruker D8 diffractometer. Measurements were conducted in Bragg–Brentano geometry with a step size of 0.01°. Phase analysis was performed using the TOPAS (v. 4.2) Rietveld refinement software, with reference data from the ICDD database.

To analyze the evolution of RA during deformation, interrupted tensile tests were performed. The specimens were unloaded at selected strain levels and subsequently examined by XRD. Prior to testing, gauge marks were introduced at 1 mm intervals along the gauge length, enabling accurate determination of the local strain corresponding to each XRD measurement.

sections.heading: Thermodynamical simulations
paragraphs: The equilibrium phase diagram of the analyzed steel, along with the temperature-dependent evolution of carbide chemical composition, as well as phase transformations during tempering and intercritical annealing, were simulated using the JMatPro software (Public Release Version 14.1, Materials Property Simulation Package).

Unless otherwise stated, all graphical representations are illustrative of representative observations. Quantitative data reported throughout the manuscript are based on statistical analyses performed over multiple representative regions of each specimen to ensure the robustness of the reported results.

sections.heading: Mechanical response and associated phase evolution
paragraphs:
The most fundamental and important indicator of the influence of the pre-annealed microstructural state on steel is the result of the static tensile test.  Fig. 2 
                          clearly indicates significant differences in both yield strength (YS) and strain hardening between the two samples. Sample Q 710 exhibits a YS of 636 ± 5 MPa, followed by pronounced strain hardening, reaching an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 990 ± 7 MPa at a uniform elongation (UEl) of 28.2 ± 0.6%. Fracture occurs at a total elongation (TEl) of 36.2 ± 1%. In contrast, sample T 710 shows a YS higher by 66 MPa, while the UTS is lower by 117 MPa. The UEl is reduced by 6% and TEl is increased by 2%. Consequently, the strength–elongation product is lower by more than 2.6 GPa% for the T 710 sample. The strain hardening behavior presented in  Fig. 2 b indicates a significantly slower decrease with true strain above 0.04 for sample Q 710 compared to T 710. In terms of the strain hardening exponent ( Fig. 2 c), the Q710 sample exhibits only slightly higher values up to a true strain of approximately 0.14, beyond which the difference becomes substantially more pronounced. This behavior is fully consistent with the interrupted tensile test results (broken line in  Fig. 2 c), which show a considerably faster strain-induced transformation of retained austenite in the Q710 sample. Consequently, a substantial fraction of the transformation potential is consumed before the onset of necking, resulting in the maximum strain hardening exponent observed at a true strain of approximately 0.22.

In contrast, the T710 sample retains a significantly higher fraction of retained austenite throughout the uniform deformation range. Accordingly, the strain hardening exponent continues to increase up to the uniform elongation, indicating that retained austenite is still actively transforming at the onset of necking. Furthermore, the substantial amount of retained austenite remaining at the end of uniform deformation suggests that a significant fraction of the transformation potential is still available during localized deformation. Consequently, the continued strain-induced transformation during necking is likely to contribute to the increased post-uniform deformation, resulting in a larger difference between the total elongation (TEl) and the uniform elongation (UEl). Such behavior has also been reported for medium-Mn steels containing highly stable retained austenite [ 47 ]. These observations directly confirm the higher mechanical stability of retained austenite in the pre-tempered condition, limiting its effective contribution during uniform deformation [ 48 , 49 ]. On the tensile curve of the Q710 sample, inhomogeneous deformation (serrations) is also visible. They are classified as a Dynamic Strain Aging (DSA) effect [ 50 ], and have also been observed in medium-Mn steels, where RA was extensively transformed into martensite during deformation [ 47 , 51 ].

The dilatometric results of heat treatment performed under identical conditions as for tensile samples are present in  Fig. 3 
                         . The dilatometric soaking curves in  Fig. 3 a clearly show that, in the Q 710 sample, the contraction during soaking is more pronounced than in the sample subjected to intercritical annealing after prior tempering. This may suggest the formation of a larger amount of austenite in this sample; however, it may also result from the combined effect of austenite formation and carbide precipitation, which in sample T710 occurred at an earlier stage of the heat treatment. In contrast, the dilatometric cooling curves ( Fig. 3 b) overlap for both samples, indicating similar RA content and no detectable phase transformation during cooling.

To further highlight the effect of prior heat treatment on austenite stability, additional annealing experiments were conducted at increased soaking temperature of 760 °C ( Fig. 3 d–f). The increased temperature was intended to generate a higher fraction of austenite, which due to its lower stability, was expected to undergo at least partial transformation during subsequent cooling [ 16 ]. In these experiments, differences in the dilatometric response during heating and cooling, depending on the initial state, are clearly visible. In the Q 760 sample, during heating ( Fig. 3 c), a decrease in the slope of the expansion curve is observed at approximately 500 °C, indicating the onset of tempering and therefore carbides precipitation. This effect is not present in the T 760 sample, as tempering had already occurred during the prior heat treatment step. The magnified view of the intercritical region in  Fig. 3 d indicates that the contraction of the sample, associated with austenite formation, begins more than 10 °C higher in the previously tempered sample. This may be associated with the depletion of the matrix in carbon and manganese due to carbide formation during tempering, which slightly increases the critical temperatures.

Fig. 3 e confirms the previous observations that the austenitic formation is more intense in quenched sample. However, in the case of annealing at elevated temperature, a significant portion of the processes (like austenite formation and carbides precipitation and further dissolution) may have already occurred during heating; therefore, the observed differences are much smaller than in the case of annealing at 710 °C. The cooling curves ( Fig. 3 f) indicate lower austenite stability in the Q 760 sample, as evidenced by an Ms temperature higher by nearly 15 °C compared to the sample tempered prior to intercritical annealing. The transformation also proceeds more intensively, as indicated by the steeper slope of the curve. This is consistent with the analysis of the strain hardening behavior obtained from the static tensile test, which indicates a more pronounced contribution of transforming, less stable RA to the strength and ductility of the steel.

Further analysis of the RA was performed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) data ( Fig. 4 
                         ). In the initial state, Q sample is characterized by the absence of detectable RA ( Fig. 4 a) and exhibits a pronounced shift of the α(110) reflection towards lower 2θ values ( Fig. 4 b), accompanied by significant peak broadening. This indicates an expanded and highly distorted lattice, consistent with a martensitic structure containing a high effective carbon content and a high level of microstrain [ 52 ]. In contrast, T sample contains a small but detectable fraction of RA, despite the process being conducted well below the Ac 1  temperature. The α peak occurs at higher 2θ with substantially reduced broadening, reflecting a lower degree of lattice distortion and a reduced effective carbon content in the α phase [ 53 ]. These features are consistent with tempering, involving carbon redistribution and partial relaxation of the martensitic structure [ 54 ].

Following intercritical annealing, both Q 710 and T 710 exhibit a marked increase in RA fraction, as evidenced by the significantly higher integrated intensities of the γ reflections ( Fig. 4 a). RA fraction for the Q710 sample reaches over 30%, while for the T710 sample it is about 5% lower ( Fig. 4 c), which is consistent with the less pronounced specimen contraction observed during dilatometric soaking, indicating a greater extent of austenite formation. Importantly, the γ peaks in both conditions are shifted towards lower 2θ compared to T sample, indicating an increased lattice parameter and, consequently, a higher effective carbon content in the austenite [ 55 ]. The similarity in γ peak positions between Q 710 and T 710 suggests that the austenite stable after final cooling reaches a comparable level of carbon enrichment regardless of the initial state. This result suggests that the increase in Ms temperature observed for sample Q 760 cannot be attributed to carbon redistribution. Simultaneously, the α(110) reflections in Q 710 and T 710 shift towards higher 2θ relative to Q sample ( Fig. 4 b), indicating a reduction in lattice parameter and, by implication, a decrease in the effective carbon content within the α phase. This behavior is consistent with carbon partitioning from martensite into austenite during intercritical treatment [ 56 , 57 ]. The peak broadening is also reduced compared to Q sample, pointing to partial relaxation of microstrain.

To clarify the presence of RA in the T sample, thermodynamic calculations were performed using JMatPro software. The equilibrium diagram indicates the presence of a small fraction of RA starting from approximately 530 °C ( Fig. 5 
                         a), reaching about 6% at 600 °C. Additionally, the carbides present at 600 °C are predominantly M 7 C 3 , along with cementite, both enriched in Mn (over 40%) and containing approximately 10% C ( Fig. 5 b). The tempering simulation suggests that the initial stage of the process is dominated by cementite precipitation ( Fig. 5 c). After approximately 200 s of tempering, cementite is predicted to be partially replaced by M 7 C 3 . Concurrently with the formation of M 7 C 3 , a small fraction of austenite is expected to form within the microstructure. Intercritical annealing of the tempered sample is predicted to result in a slight decrease in carbide fraction and the formation of up to 7% RA ( Fig. 5 d); however, this is not consistent with the experimental XRD results. In the case of the sample annealed directly after quenching, the simulation indicates a very similar evolution of cementite and austenite, without the presence of M 7 C 3  ( Fig. 5 e). The results of the thermodynamic calculations therefore suggest the possibility of forming a small amount of austenite at 600 °C. Although the equilibrium simulations do not quantitatively reproduce all experimentally observed features, particularly the retained austenite fraction after the final intercritical annealing stage, they correctly capture several important transformation tendencies, including the possible formation of a small amount of austenite during tempering and the precipitation of carbides. Therefore, consistent with our previous experience and earlier studies on medium-Mn steels [ 58 ], the thermodynamic calculations were used primarily to identify equilibrium phase tendencies and possible transformation paths rather than to provide quantitative predictions of the final microstructure. To further verify the predicted formation of austenite during tempering, additional dilatometric experiments were performed using a substantially reduced heating rate. Therefore, thermodynamic calculations are used here primarily to indicate equilibrium tendencies, whereas the experimentally observed microstructure results from non-equilibrium continuous annealing.

As initially applied heating rate of 3 °C is far from equilibrium conditions assumed in simulations, an additional dilatometric test was performed using a very low heating rate. Slower heating promotes conditions closer to thermodynamic equilibrium, and previous studies have shown that this is also associated with a reduction in the critical temperatures Ac 1  and Ac 3  [ 59 ].  Fig. 6 
                          presents the dilatometric curve for a sample heated at a rate of 200 °C/h (0.05 °C/s). The main austenitic transformation begins at above 650 °C (2 in  Fig. 6 ), which is comparable to the values obtained during heating at 3 °C/s. However, already slightly above 600 °C a small contraction of the sample can be observed (1 in  Fig. 6 ), consistent with the XRD results and thermodynamic prediction of the possible formation of a small amount of austenite during tempering. This effect may be associated with the local formation of austenite, for example in regions exhibiting elemental segregation, which has been reported in medium-Mn steel [ 60 ] and may be further enhanced by the tempering step.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization, phase composition and chemical redistribution
paragraphs: The microstructure of the Q710 ( Fig. 7 g) sample is typical of properly intercritically annealed hot-rolled medium-Mn steel [ 18 , 19 ]. Homogeneous, bright, lath-like RA grains are distributed within a darker ferritic matrix, resulting in a hardness of 291 HV1. No irregular features are observed within the RA grains that could indicate martensite formation during cooling or subsequent sample preparation. This observation is consistent with the dilatometric results, which show no detectable phase transformation during cooling from 710 °C. The IPF map ( Fig. 7 h) allows the distinction of two prior austenite grains, within which the ART-formed RA adopts the same crystallographic orientation [ 64 ]. The use of the UGC map shows that some RA grains remain individual, while others have merged to form a complex network ( Fig. 7 i). This is attributed to the nucleation and growth of austenite along the boundaries of pre-existing martensite.

Due to the preservation of the same crystallographic orientation within the prior austenite grain, when two austenite growth fronts meet, the grains coalesce [ 49 ], forming a complex network around the former martensite grains. Grain boundary misorientations are predominantly within the range of 42–47°, corresponding to the ferrite–austenite orientation relationship [ 65 ], whereas low- and high-angle boundaries associated with the initial martensitic microstructure are rarely observed ( Fig. 8 ).

Although the matrix microstructures are very similar, the retained austenite exhibits pronounced differences. Distinct zones can be identified within the RA regions of T 710 sample ( Fig. 7 j). The outer shell appears typical of RA, whereas the core, based on the etching response, does not resemble RA. At the same time, it does not exhibit martensitic characteristics, as no typical martensitic laths are observed, and it shows the lowest hardness among all samples (284 HV1). This interpretation is further supported by the dilatometric results, which reveal no detectable martensitic transformation during cooling from 710 °C. Instead, its morphology is more similar to ferrite. The central part of some RA regions again resembles typical RA. Additionally, in some areas, rounded features are observed, which may correspond to undissolved precipitates. EBSD indicates that RA in sample T710 exhibits a significantly smaller grain size (surface area) ( Fig. 7 k and l), which is confirmed by the quantitative analysis presented in  Fig. 9 
                         a. In sample T710, grains with an area of approximately 0.7 μm 2  are most frequent, whereas in sample Q710 the grain area ranges from about 2 to 90 μm 2 . In T 710 sample as well, RA inherits the crystallographic orientation from the prior austenite. The most significant observation is presented in  Fig. 7 l. Both intercritically annealed samples exhibit a comparable RA content (with a difference of approximately 5%). However, in contrast to the typical RA network [ 66 ] observed in sample Q710, the RA in sample T710 consists of significantly smaller grains that are also largely isolated from one another. This effect is illustrated in  Fig. 9 b, where the number of individual grains is plotted as a function of their area. The T710 sample contains several times more individual RA grains despite the similar overall retained austenite fraction. This is further supported by the noticeably higher fraction of grain boundaries with misorientation angles other than 42–47° ( Fig. 8 b–d), indicating restricted RA growth along martensite boundaries. This result suggests that carbides formed during tempering limit the growth potential of austenite during annealing.

It should be emphasized that the observed mechanical response cannot be attributed solely to retained austenite morphology. Rather, it reflects the combined influence of retained austenite fraction, chemical composition, morphology, and characteristic dimensions, all of which contribute to its mechanical stability [ 9 ]. In the present work, these effects are consistently reflected by the experimentally determined Ms temperature, which is lower for the T710 condition and agrees with the interrupted tensile tests and microstructural observations.

Further TEM analysis were performed to identify specific phases ( Fig. 12 
                         ). TEM microdiffraction allowed the precipitates in the T sample to be identified as cementite ( Fig. 12 b) located in ferritic matrix ( Fig. 12 c). After annealing at 710 °C for 40 s, the microstructure consisted predominantly of ferrite and austenite laths ( Fig. 12 d,e,g). However, the presence of undissolved carbide precipitates within the RA laths was still confirmed ( Fig. 12 f), indicating incomplete carbide dissolution during intercritical annealing.

sections.heading: Effect of pre-tempering on austenite morphology and stability
paragraphs: The Q710 sample exhibits a typical microstructural morphology, grain size, and mechanical behavior under tensile loading. The presence of carbide precipitates in samples T and T710 significantly influences the nucleation, growth, and chemo-mechanical properties of austenite. To better elucidate these effects, further targeted investigations were conducted.

Fig. 13 
                          presents higher-magnification EBSD maps. The differences between the Q 710 and T 710 samples are clearly visible. In the Q 710 sample, RA grains are elongated, with rounded shapes, and form interconnected networks with neighboring grains ( Fig. 13 a–c). The microstructure is dominated by boundaries of approximately 45° ( Fig. 13 e). In contrast, in the T710 sample, the grains are more fragmented, with much smaller surface areas and highly irregular, jagged morphologies. They do not form interconnected networks but rather occur as isolated, small grains ( Fig. 13 b–d), resulting in a visibly higher fraction of α/α grain boundaries within the microstructure ( Fig. 13 f).

The observed morphology of RA could suggest the occurrence of a martensitic transformation during heat treatment, which would lead to fragmentation of RA [ 67 , 68 ]. However, the analysis of IQ values does not support this scenario. In regions containing martensite, IQ values would be expected to be significantly lower than those of the ferritic matrix [ 69 ]; however, the entire α-phase exhibits comparable IQ values. Furthermore, this was quantitatively analyzed in the plot shown in  Fig. 14 
                         a. The results indicate the absence of a bimodal IQ distribution for ferrite, which could otherwise suggest the presence of martensite. The IQ values for the Q 710 and T 710 samples are nearly identical. Moreover, the IQ values for ferrite are consistently higher than those for RA in both samples. The presence of martensite is also not supported by the relatively low hardness of the T710 sample, which is even lower than that of the Q710 sample ( Fig. 14 b). A small fraction of martensite, or even austenite with critically low stability, would be expected to result in a noticeable increase in hardness, as observed in earlier investigations [ 16 , 70 ].

Further analyses of T 710 sample were performed on a lamella to ensure the highest accuracy and to eliminate potential artefacts resulting from standard mechanical sample preparation. In this case, it was possible to relatively clearly identify regions of the α phase that, under standard conditions, could be considered parts of bigger austenite grains (indicated by blue/black/white arrows in  Fig. 15 
                         ). Some of these regions indeed exhibit lower IQ values, as well as elevated KAM values and even distinctly different crystallographic orientations compared to the ferritic matrix. However, there are also areas that are otherwise similar but show IQ and KAM values comparable to the matrix. This does not allow for an unambiguous confirmation of the presence of martensite The similar orientation of the RA grains suggests that they originate from a single prior austenite grain.

From the lamella shown in  Fig. 15 , two regions characteristic of RA features observed by SEM were selected and further magnified in  Fig. 16 
                         : (a) an inhomogeneous RA grain, and (b) RA containing carbide precipitates. STEM imaging in  Fig. 16 c clearly indicates the dual nature of the inhomogeneous RA grain. TEM-EDS results show that the outer part of the grain is strongly enriched in Mn and depleted in Al, whereas the inner region exhibits Mn and Al levels comparable to the matrix ( Fig. 16 c). For the remaining alloying elements, the differences are below the detection limit. The TKD map for this area clearly indicates that the inner part of the RA grain belongs to the α phase ( Fig. 16 e) and exhibits elevated KAM values ( Fig. 16 f). Moreover, it shows a distinctly different crystallographic orientation and is separated from the ferritic matrix by a high-angle grain boundary ( Fig. 16 g–k) exceeding 50° ( Fig. 17 
                         a). Line scan analyses indicate that the matrix–RA boundaries exhibit a misorientation angle of approximately 45° ( Fig. 16 k). The ferritic matrix shows the highest IQ values, while RA exhibits the lowest. The unidentified α phase inside RA grain exhibits intermediate IQ values, suggesting that it is not martensite ( Fig. 17 ).

The RA region containing an undissolved carbide precipitate is shown in the STEM image in  Fig. 16 d. EDS analysis clearly indicates that the RA lath is significantly enriched in Mn compared to the matrix; however, the precipitates contain much higher concentrations of this element, as well as C. Carbides are strongly depleted in Al. The precipitate was not captured in the EBSD scan, neither in phase analysis nor in crystallographic orientation ( Fig. 16 h–j); however, elevated KAM values are observed in its vicinity ( Fig. 16 i). For this region, again IQ values are much lower for RA than for the matrix.

TEM and HR-TEM ( Fig. 17 ) were used to provide detailed characterization of the selected areas of interest.  Fig. 17 a and b include markings (1–3) indicating the individual features analyzed. Bright-field (a) and dark-field (b, c) images reveal three characteristic features with distinct contrast and morphology. Feature 2 corresponds to an inhomogeneous grain located inside RA, as shown in (d). Higher magnification HR-TEM images (e, f) display well-defined lattice fringes within the RA region, indicating locally ordered atomic planes. The parallel yellow lines mark the directions of atomic rows and enable a qualitative assessment of crystallographic relationships and local lattice distortions. In region 2_1 ( Fig. 17 e), the atomic rows marked by the yellow lines exhibit the same orientation within the central part of the grain, spanning both the RA and the ferrite. This indicates a locally coherent or near-coherent relationship between the phases. However, toward the outer region 2_1 ( Fig. 17 f), the orientation of the atomic rows in RA and the surrounding ferritic matrix differs, suggesting a loss of coherency and the presence of misorientation at the interface. Feature 3 is identified as a carbide particle (Fe 3 C) embedded within the RA, as evidenced in (g–i). The HR-TEM images (h, i) show a distinct interface between Fe 3 C and the surrounding matrix, with lattice fringes visible on both sides. However, the orientation of atomic rows is not continuous across the interface, indicating a semi-coherent or incoherent character of the Fe 3 C/RA interface.

It should be noted that the analysis of a single HR-TEM lamella cannot provide statistically representative information on the prevalence of the observed microstructural features. However, the regions selected for HR-TEM investigation were not isolated observations but were chosen based on characteristic features that had already been identified by SEM ( Fig. 7 j) and were repeatedly observed throughout the investigated specimens. Although a statistically resolved spatial correlation between individual carbide precipitates and locally arrested austenite growth was beyond the scope of the present study, the comparative microstructural evolution presented in  Fig. 7  provides clear qualitative evidence of their relationship. In the Q710 sample, where no carbide precipitates were present prior to intercritical annealing, retained austenite developed as a relatively continuous network. In contrast, pre-tempering produced chains of carbide precipitates located predominantly along prior martensitic boundaries, and the subsequently reverted austenite formed in these regions exhibited a markedly finer, fragmented, and morphologically discontinuous character. Owing to the extensive dissolution of carbides during intercritical annealing and the submicrometre dimensions of the relevant microstructural features, establishing a statistically representative spatial correlation using conventional chemical mapping techniques is highly challenging. Nevertheless, the systematic differences observed between the Q710 and T710 microstructures indicate a clear relationship between the presence of carbide precipitates prior to annealing and the altered morphology of the reverted austenite. Moreover, the proposed interpretation is supported by complementary evidence obtained from EBSD, EDS, XRD, dilatometry, and mechanical testing. Therefore, the HR-TEM observations should be regarded as high-resolution confirmation of representative microstructural features rather than the sole basis for the proposed transformation mechanism.

sections.heading: Origin of inhomogeneous RA: a role of carbide-induced chemical heterogeneity
paragraphs: The inhomogeneous austenite-related features observed in the T710 sample cannot be readily explained within the conventional framework of austenite reversion in medium-Mn steels, which typically assumes chemically homogeneous initial conditions and continuous phase transformation. In particular, the presence of irregular regions embedded within or partially enclosed by retained austenite, together with pronounced chemical gradients and complex grain morphologies, indicates that the transformation deviates from the conventional continuous reversion process. However, based on the available experimental evidence, it is not possible to unequivocally determine whether these regions correspond to untransformed ferrite or to martensite formed during cooling.

Accordingly, two possible mechanisms are considered ( Fig. 18 
                         ): (i) spatially heterogeneous austenite formation with locally restricted growth ( Fig. 18 a–c), and (ii) partial martensitic transformation of initially formed austenite ( Fig. 18 d–f). Both mechanisms are consistent with some of the experimental observations and were therefore evaluated using the combined results of SEM, EBSD, TEM/EDS, XRD, dilatometry, mechanical testing, and relevant literature. Although the available evidence does not allow the alternative mechanism to be completely excluded, the combined experimental observations provide stronger support for diffusion-limited austenite growth under chemically heterogeneous conditions than for partial martensitic transformation:

In contrast to the commonly assumed chemically homogeneous initial condition in medium-Mn steels, the introduction of a pre-tempering step leads to the formation of Mn-enriched carbides and pronounced microscale chemical heterogeneity. As demonstrated by Liu et al. [ 71 ], such carbides play a dual role during intercritical annealing: they act as preferential nucleation sites for austenite while simultaneously reducing the growth rate due to Mn depletion in the surrounding matrix. This appears to alter the balance between nucleation and growth kinetics. This effect is further amplified in medium-Mn steels, where the inherently sluggish diffusion of Mn enhances the sensitivity of the transformation process to local compositional variations [ 72 ]. Recent studies have shown that the dissolution behavior and chemical composition of carbides play a critical role in determining the kinetics of austenite formation and the final RA fraction [ 18 ]. In particular, coarse carbides enriched in Mn tend to dissolve more slowly, thereby acting as persistent sinks for solute atoms and limiting the availability of Mn required for austenite stabilization.

Importantly, the combined experimental results indicate that carbide-induced chemical heterogeneity does not merely reduce the austenite fraction or modify its stability, as typically reported, but can modify the transformation pathway, leading to the formation of partially transformed regions within individual grains. These observations are consistent with a transformation pathway that has not been explicitly discussed in previous studies. This effect may be further reinforced by Al partitioning. Since Al is a ferrite stabilizer and is rejected from cementite and austenite, local Al enrichment in the surrounding α matrix may additionally increase the thermodynamic resistance to austenite formation [ 73 , 74 ]. Thus, the carbide-induced chemical field should not be considered only as Mn/C enrichment around carbides, but also as a coupled Mn–C–Al redistribution, where Mn and C locally promote austenite formation, whereas Al locally favors the persistence of α. A comparable relationship between local compositional heterogeneity and hierarchical microstructural development has also been reported in other alloy systems, where localized chemical partitioning governed the spatial evolution of individual phases, although through different transformation mechanisms [ 75 , 76 ].

The growth of austenite during intercritical annealing is controlled by the transport of Mn from ferrite to austenite. However, due to extremely low bulk diffusion coefficients of Mn at intercritical temperatures, this process relies predominantly on short-circuit diffusion pathways, including grain boundaries, dislocations, and their associated migration processes [ 77 ]. These pathways provide localized channels for rapid Mn transport, enabling austenite growth under otherwise diffusion-limited conditions. Importantly, the efficiency of these mechanisms is highly sensitive to the local microstructure, including grain boundary character, dislocation density, and the presence of second-phase particles. Consequently, Mn transport—and therefore austenite growth—is inherently spatially heterogeneous.

In the present microstructure, the combined effect of carbide-induced chemical heterogeneity and spatially variable diffusion pathways results in non-uniform advancement of the austenite/ferrite interface. Regions with sufficient Mn supply, facilitated by grain boundary or dislocation-assisted diffusion, may evolve under conditions approaching partitioning local equilibrium (PLE), allowing enrichment and stabilization of austenite. In contrast, regions depleted in Mn due to the presence of carbides are forced toward negligible partitioning local equilibrium (NPLE)-like conditions, where substitutional diffusion is suppressed and only limited transformation can occur. Moreover, recent studies indicate that the α/γ interface mobility itself can be locally reduced or fluctuate due to interactions with precipitates and compositional gradients [ 26 ], further contributing to spatially non-uniform transformation kinetics. As a result, different regions of the same grain may evolve under distinct transformation regimes, leading to the coexistence of Mn-enriched austenite and Mn-lean or untransformed α-phase, as illustrated in  Fig. 18 a–c. This interpretation is consistent with observations of compositional gradients and core–shell structures in RA reported in medium-Mn steels [ 78 ]. In such cases, Mn-enriched shells surrounding lower-Mn cores stabilize austenite against martensitic transformation. However, in previously reported systems, the austenite remains crystallographically continuous despite compositional variation. In contrast, the present results demonstrate that sufficiently strong chemical heterogeneity can disrupt not only the composition but also the spatial continuity of the transformed phase, leading to a microstructure that cannot be described as fully developed austenite.

The HR-TEM observations provide direct atomic-scale evidence supporting this interpretation. The presence of locally aligned atomic rows across the RA/F interface indicates that the transformation initially proceeds under near-coherent conditions. However, this coherency is progressively lost toward the outer regions, where significant misorientation of atomic rows is observed. Such a transition from coherent to incoherent interface conditions is characteristic of diffusion-controlled transformations under increasing lattice misfit and compositional gradients. Furthermore, the presence of Fe 3 C particles embedded within the austenite introduces additional constraints on interface mobility. The semi-coherent or incoherent nature of the Fe 3 C/RA interfaces suggests that these particles act as pinning points, locally hindering interface migration and contributing to the arrest of austenite growth.

An alternative explanation for the observed inhomogeneous features is the partial transformation of austenite into martensite, particularly in Mn-lean regions with reduced stability ( Fig. 18 d–f). While such behavior has been reported in chemically heterogeneous systems [ 79 ], it is not supported by the present experimental evidence. Specifically, the absence of a bimodal IQ distribution, the relatively low KAM values, the lack of hardness increase, and the absence of transformation signals in dilatometric measurements all argue against the presence of martensite. Therefore, the α-phase regions observed within the austenite are interpreted as untransformed regions rather than martensitic products.

The present findings therefore extend the current understanding of austenite reversion in medium-Mn steels by demonstrating that chemical heterogeneity can influence not only the kinetics and stability of austenite, but also the spatial continuity and completeness of phase transformation. While previous studies [ 26 , 74 , 77 ] have established the importance of Mn partitioning, short-circuit diffusion, and carbide effects, they have not demonstrated that these factors can lead to locally arrested transformation and the formation of partially transformed grains. In this context, the observed microstructure represents a distinct transformation regime characterized by the coexistence of PLE- and NPLE-controlled regions within a single grain and by interruption of the transformation front due to combined chemical and microstructural constraints. The inhomogeneous RA observed in the T710 sample is therefore interpreted as a manifestation of diffusion-limited, spatially heterogeneous transformation governed by carbide-induced chemical gradients and localized diffusion pathways, leading to locally arrested austenite growth rather than martensitic transformation.

Beyond the mechanistic considerations regarding the origin of the observed inhomogeneity, the most critical aspect is the clear difference in microstructural morphology, as reflected by the contrast between the continuous austenite network in the Q710 condition and the fragmented, spatially discontinuous morphology observed in the T710 sample. More importantly, these morphological differences are directly associated with distinct mechanical responses, which ultimately determine the applicability of the material in industrial conditions. In particular, the continuity, stability, and distribution of RA are known to govern the effectiveness of the TRIP effect, strain hardening behavior, and damage tolerance. Therefore, the transition from a continuous to a fragmented austenite morphology, as rationalized in  Fig. 18 , must be considered a key factor in the process design. These findings highlight that, beyond thermodynamic and kinetic considerations, the control of microstructural heterogeneity and transformation completeness is essential for tailoring mechanical performance and must be explicitly taken into account when designing industrial processing routes for advanced multiphase medium-Mn steels.

The present study should not be interpreted as establishing a universal processing route for medium-Mn steels. Instead, it demonstrates how pre-tempering modifies the subsequent intercritical annealing response under the investigated processing conditions. Although the proposed mechanism is expected to be relevant whenever carbide-induced chemical heterogeneity develops prior to austenite reversion, its applicability to different alloy compositions and processing schedules requires further systematic investigation. From an industrial perspective, pre-tempering should be regarded as a tool for tailoring the balance between strength, retained austenite stability, and strain-hardening behavior rather than as an inherently beneficial or detrimental processing step.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
This study investigated the effect of pre-tempering followed by intercritical annealing on the morphology, stability, and mechanical response of retained austenite in an Al-alloyed medium-Mn steel. The main conclusions are as follows: 
                         
                            • 
                            Pre-tempering produced Mn-enriched carbide precipitates and local chemical heterogeneity, which modified the initial microstructural state prior to intercritical annealing. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            Compared with direct intercritical annealing, the pre-tempered condition resulted in a lower retained austenite fraction, finer and less continuous retained austenite morphology, and higher austenite stability, leading to a modified strain-hardening response despite similar overall mechanical performance. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            The combined results obtained from dilatometry, XRD, EBSD, TEM/EDS, and mechanical testing indicate that the observed microstructure cannot be fully explained by the conventional concept of homogeneous austenite reversion. Among the two mechanisms considered, the experimental evidence provides stronger support for spatially heterogeneous, diffusion-limited austenite growth than for partial martensitic transformation during cooling. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            The results indicate that carbide-induced chemical heterogeneity can significantly influence the austenite reversion pathway under continuous annealing conditions and should therefore be considered in the design and optimization of heat treatment schedules for medium-Mn steels.
